paragraphs: Conclusion | The core difference between this occupation (U.S. SOC 17-1022.01, geodetic surveyors) and adjacent roles lies in “scale, accuracy and levels of authorization”: this occupation focuses on large-area Earth reference frameworks, high-accuracy control networks, datum transformations, coordinates and elevations, producing control results, coordinates, elevations, databases and quality descriptions; land surveyors (17-1022.00) primarily survey parcels, ownership and engineering projects; cartographers/photogrammetrists (17-1021.00) primarily work on maps, imagery, photogrammetry and geographic visualization; geographic information technicians primarily manage/analyze spatial data, create maps and work with systems; civil engineers (17-2051.00) focus on structural design, construction and acceptance; data scientists (15-2051.00) focus on statistics, machine learning and data modeling. Scales and levels of authorization differ; authority for ownership conclusions, engineering acceptance or classified-deliverable approval cannot be carried over across roles.

Introduction | The following comparison uses four columns: “career direction—core work and outputs—key differences—choices it may better suit”. Geodesy, land surveying, cartography, geographic information, civil engineering design and data analysis often connect within the same surveying/mapping or engineering system, but connections do not make them interchangeable. When moving between directions, learn the new direction’s datums, standards, qualifications, authorization and responsibility boundaries.

This occupation emphasizes large-area control and datums; other directions emphasize boundaries, maps, systems, structures or statistics. Work may overlap, with specific responsibilities divided by project and license; titles cannot rule out control or database tasks.

May better suit people willing to work over the long term with spatial datums, high-accuracy observations and coordinate calculations, maintain rigor about accuracy, specifications and check conditions, and accept equal emphasis on field and office work.

Core work and outputs: analyze control or survey data for compliance with project specifications or land surveying standards; survey large areas of the Earth's surface using satellite observations, GNSS, LIDAR or related methods; calculate precise horizontal and vertical positions of surface points; maintain geodetic, coordinate and quality databases and verify data correctness; compute horizontal and vertical control-network coordinates using direct leveling, triangulation, trilateration, traversing or other techniques; plan or direct survey personnel; assess control-data quality and determine whether additional observations are required; outputs include control results, coordinates, elevations, databases and quality descriptions (U.S. SOC 17-1022.01).
This occupation: geodetic surveyors (17-1022.01)

Land surveying emphasizes boundaries and legal land documents, while this occupation emphasizes large-area control; its official tasks also include land grids and parcel orientation. Check licenses and responsibilities separately for boundary surveys, certification of legal documents and judicial determination of ownership.

May better suit people willing to work on parcels, ownership and engineering setting-out and accept legal/ownership boundary responsibilities; this occupation focuses more on large-area control, datums and high-accuracy coordinates.

Core work and outputs: define parcels/boundaries and perform ownership surveys and engineering setting-out; conduct topographic/as-built surveys and issue survey records and drawings; support ownership registration and dispute handling; outputs include ownership, boundary, setting-out and as-built survey records.
Land surveyors (Surveyors, 17-1022.00)

Key difference: cartographers/photogrammetrists focus on map design, image processing, photogrammetric computations and geographic visualization, producing maps and imagery deliverables; this occupation focuses on control networks, datums, coordinates and elevations, with maps/imagery usually as downstream applications.
May better suit people willing to work in map design, image processing and visualization; this occupation focuses more on control, datums, coordinates and elevations.

Core work and outputs: process aerial/satellite imagery, perform photogrammetric computations and three-dimensional reconstruction, design map symbols/layouts, compile maps and thematic maps, and maintain geographic visualization products; outputs include maps, imagery deliverables and photogrammetry reports.
Cartographers and Photogrammetrists (17-1021.00)

GIS technicians emphasize spatial databases and system analysis; this occupation also maintains geodetic databases. Scope and platform operations/maintenance responsibilities follow the actual division of work and are not categorically excluded by titles.
May better suit people willing to work in spatial-data management, analysis, cartography and system applications; this occupation focuses more on field observations, control and datums.

Core work and outputs: build/maintain spatial databases and data models, perform spatial queries, overlay, network/statistical analysis and cartography, and support business, planning and decision applications; outputs include spatial datasets, analysis results and maps.
Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians

Key difference: civil engineers focus on structural design, loads, materials, construction and acceptance, producing design drawings and calculation reports; this occupation provides control, terrain and coordinate information for engineering design and usually does not take responsibility for structural safety or engineering acceptance.
May better suit people willing to work in structural design, construction and acceptance; this occupation focuses more on spatial datums, surveys and control deliverables.

Core work and outputs: perform structural calculations/design and draw construction plans under specifications, support construction, supervision and acceptance, and handle changes; outputs include structural designs, calculation reports and construction drawings.
Civil Engineers (17-2051.00)

Key difference: data scientists focus on statistics, machine learning, data modeling and evaluation, producing models and data products; this occupation focuses on survey observations, adjustment, coordinates and elevations, using data methods for quality analysis/assessment without models and algorithms as the main outputs.
May better suit people willing to work in statistics, machine learning and data products; this occupation focuses more on survey observations and spatial datums.

Core work and outputs: clean/integrate data, engineer features, model and validate, assess model performance, deploy/monitor data products, and explain results to business stakeholders; outputs include models, evaluations and data-product reports.
Data Scientists (15-2051.00)

Transition | This page places adjacent roles alongside each other by “scale, accuracy and levels of authorization” to help you identify which surveying, spatial-data, engineering or analysis role you want to pursue over the long term. Whichever direction you choose, actual readiness depends on its datum, standard, qualification and authorization requirements; ability to clearly record observations, calculations, deliverables and metadata; and willingness to take responsibility for accuracy, data security and clients’ rights and interests. Interest questionnaires only help raise questions.
AI tools and review responsibilities

May 2025 OEWS covers U.S. wage and salary workers. The self-employed are outside the survey scope. The published figures cover the broader occupation group. May 2025 national medians: Surveyors, broader group (17-1022): $75,440/year.

How to interpret this interest code: RIC combines Realistic (fieldwork, instrument operation and hands-on engineering work), Investigative (analyzing and investigating spatial, physical and data problems), and Conventional (organizing information and records according to standards) interests. It helps you understand preferences for this occupational direction, not predict performance. This aligns with O*NET's descriptions of its tasks (conducting surveys to determine the positions and characteristics of surface points, calculating precise horizontal and vertical positions, maintaining geodetic databases, and verifying data's mathematical correctness) and work activities (working with computers 91, processing information 90, analyzing data or information 87, getting information 87, and documenting and recording information 83).

Geodetic surveyors | Outputs include verifiable control deliverables, coordinates, elevations, databases and quality explanations: design control networks and observation plans based on datums, conduct GNSS, leveling and related observations, perform adjustment and accuracy assessment, maintain databases, and submit deliverables and metadata (U.S. SOC 17-1022.01).

See work fit evidence for the shared criteria.

Surveyors | Outputs concern parcels, ownership and engineering surveys: define parcels and boundaries, perform ownership surveys and engineering setting-out, conduct topographic and as-built surveys, and produce survey records and drawings.
Have capabilities in parcel, ownership and engineering surveying and setting-out.
If you prefer large-area control and datums over parcel and ownership surveying, this direction is not recommended.

Geographic information technicians | Outputs include spatial data management, analysis and mapping: build and maintain spatial databases and data models, perform spatial analysis and mapping, and support business and planning applications.
Have capabilities in spatial data management, analysis and mapping.
If you prefer field observations and control deliverables over data and system applications, this direction is not recommended.

Cartographers and photogrammetrists | Outputs include maps, imagery and photogrammetry: process aerial and satellite imagery, perform photogrammetric computations and three-dimensional reconstruction, design map symbols and layouts, and compile maps.
Have capabilities in image processing, photogrammetry and map design.
If you prefer control, datums, coordinates and elevations over map and imagery deliverables, this direction is not recommended.

Civil engineers | Outputs include engineering structural design and construction support: perform structural calculations and design according to standards, draw construction plans, support construction, supervision and acceptance, and handle changes.
Have capabilities in structural design, calculations and construction support.
If you prefer surveying and control deliverables over structural design and engineering acceptance, this direction is not recommended.

Data scientists | Outputs include statistics, machine learning and data modeling: clean and integrate data, perform feature engineering, modeling and validation, assess model performance, and deploy and monitor data products.
Have capabilities in statistics, machine learning and data products.
If you prefer surveying observations and spatial reference systems over statistical modeling and data products, this direction is not recommended.

Signs of fit: willingness to take responsibility for observations, calculations and deliverables within qualifications, standards and authorization; ability to work rigorously with spatial reference systems and numerical calculations over the long term; and ability to maintain checks and records under fieldwork and schedule pressure, reporting exceedances or anomalies according to procedures.

Reasons for caution: difficulty working over the long term under extremely demanding accuracy, standards and checking requirements; difficulty accepting the effects of field conditions, seasons and travel; or unwillingness to report and hand over according to procedures when qualifications or authorization are exceeded.

Validation suggestion: first use a simulated or real surveying task to test datum confirmation, plan design, observations, adjustment, deliverable submission and checking. Understand the target jurisdiction's and organization's requirements for surveying and mapping qualifications, registration, deliverables, state secrets and data security before deciding on long-term commitment.
